By classifying upfront, the solution saves significant processing overhead and latency, optimizing performance.\nA toxicity and safety filter screens for inappropriate or offensive entries, ensuring the system does not return results for queries containing abusive, hateful, or derogatory input. Tolerances for this model are configurable in total and discretely for six different types of toxicity.\nA named-entity recognition system extracts property details in the search. This can include amenities on property, such as a spa or private beach. It also recognizes attractions such as sporting events, museums or theatres. It enables intuitive filtering by price, such as “less than $400” in multiple currencies, including award points. \n\nA large language model (Google Gemini) is used to retrieve relevant world knowledge when a guest searches for new topics not stored in the enriched catalog. This includes general knowledge unrelated to specific hotels. If the guest wants to go white water rafting, the LLM will respond with the top places in the world to do that.\nAssess\nEnvision\nImplement\nActivate\nA catalogue enrichment process to cache knowledge built up from authored and user-generated content as well as past search results. This process improves the performance of future queries by reducing the need for LLM calls for repeated similar queries. Process includes human in the loop review to prevent hallucinations from entering catalogue.\nOptimize\nHow it works\nBlend developed several AI-based capabilities to enable personalized, intent-based property recommendations\nClassification\nSafety\nRecognition\nComprehension\nMemory\nSimple destination queries with no additional parameters route to existing flow saving compute\nComplex queries with features, amenities, experience use only entity extraction for low latency\nEntirely new knowledge queries (e.g., “white water rafting”) utilize the full stack of capabilities\nSystematic catalogue improvements reduce need for intensive AI calls for similar topics\nPrivate & Confidential\n\n--- SLIDE 96 ---\n\nHow the solution understands a query\nClassification\nHotels in Phoenix with swimming and tesla charging under $400\nIntent\nDestination\nAmenity\nPool\nAmenity\nEV Charger\nPrice\n< 400 USD\n1\nClassification\nAlpine ski resort for romantic honeymoon with nightclubs and spa\nIntent\nTheme\n2\nRomantic\nPhoenix\nType\nResort\nAmenity\nSpa\nAttraction\nNightclub\nActivity\nAlpine Skiing\n Listed Amenity\n Listed Amenity\n In Catalog\n In Catalog\n Listed\n Listed\n Unknown\nLLM Call\nFind top global destinations for Alpine Skiing\nLLM Destination Response\nFrench Alps: Three Valleys; Chamonix; Courchevel\nSwiss Alps: Zermatt; Verbier; St. Mortitz\nAustrian Alps: St Anton am Alrberg; Kitzbühel; Ischgl\nItalian Alps: Cortina d’Ampezzo; Madonna di Campiglio; Cervinia\nPrivate & Confidential\nSafe\nSafe\n\n--- SLIDE 97 ---\n\nSynthetic Training Data\nNo prior history data was available for training and tuning models. We could support everyday but also do quarterly reviews in-depth]\n\n--- SLIDE 38 ---\n\nROI Calculation is an Extension of Model Development\nValue / Cost = ROI\n\nThis is pretty easy math, right? ROI is just the value that I got for my spend divided by the spend. \nHowever, there can be variants of ROI\nDifferent Flavors of ROI\n\nRetail Sales ROI = $ Sales / Cost\n\nGM ROI = Gross Margin $ / Cost\n\nIf sales data can be segmented then Segment ROIs are possible\nLong Term ROI\n\nLong Term ROI refers to understanding that media, especially upper funnel media like Branded OTT, has a longer-term brand equity impact. \n\nLong Term ROI is far more directional in nature than the typical ROI (short-term) that comes out of MMM\t \n\n--- SLIDE 39 ---\n\nLT ROI Leverages the “Base” \nAn MMM doesn’t attempt to explain 100% of sales; it estimates the portion caused by Media, Price, and Trade.  \nThe remaining, unexplained portion is termed the Base, or Non-Media Driven sales\nWe’ll use this to estimate long-term effects\n\n--- SLIDE 40 ---\n\nLong-Term Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM) \nIn a typical MMM, media data is decayed anywhere from 4-13 weeks.\n\nWhen Brands ask, “what’s in ‘non-media’ or Base”, part of answer is always “long-term value of Brand”.\n\nA simple way to estimate this is to test lags of media (3 / 6/ 9 / 12 month) against a 3-5 year baseline from an MMM.  \n\n--- SLIDE 41 ---\n\nTwo-Stage uses Equity Tracking data\nShort-Term\nMedia \nEffect\nEquity \nEffect\nEquity ROI + Short-Term ROI = Total ROI\nHere we layer onto our MMM by first estimating media’s impact on Equity data – note statistical rigor has to be relaxed for this due to data sparsity (directional!)  We then estimate the Equity impact on our long-term Base to determine how media drove a long-term effect\n\n--- SLIDE 42 ---\n\n     Data Science Expertise\nThe data scientists at our competitors know how to run the standard automated code that is given to them to by their company – they don’t understand how to build custom models like those needed for Reynolds American\nWe’re also AI experts, ready to leverage the best of evolving capabilities when RA is ready for them\n\n     Joint Model Development Drives Adoption\nMaking Marketing & Finance teams part of the solution creates confidence in using the models to make decisions\n\n      Flexible Approach can Change in the Future\nImplement somebody else’s solution and you’ll be stuck with the model that gets implemented; The model allows each component DMA to have it’s own response, which then builds up the State level effect.  This is powerful; instead of have 5,200 observations (50 states x 104 weeks) our model will have over 21,840 observations (210 DMA x 104 weeks plus DMA / State overlaps)\n \nFor Reynolds American, we would look at DMA-within-State differences to create an estimate of State level effects; State effects would create the Total US estimate\nFixed and Random Effects\nState \nEffect\nDMA\nDMA\nDMA\n\n--- SLIDE 86 ---\n\nMMM Methodology and Forms Vary by Business Situation\nModel Forms\nAdditive\t\t\t\nMultiplicative\nLog-Log / Log-Linear\n|  Advanced Measurement With Blend360\nMethodologies\nOrdinary Least Squares\nHierarchical Regression\nBayesian Regression\nVARx\nUnobserved Components Model\nMulti-model Approaches \u000b(ex – Facebook Robyn Model)\nPrivate and Confidential\n\n--- SLIDE 87 ---\n\nWhat’s the difference between ROI and ROAS?  \nTypically, ROAS or Return on Ad Spend, is used in media platforms that that measure campaign effectiveness for specific campaigns served via that platform.\nROAS tends to denote that the view is limited to what is available in that platform and not inclusive of all the effects that an MMM will measure\nROI v ROAS, Channels v Campaigns\nWhy aren’t Campaigns in MMM?  Why only Channels?\nThe short answer is that MMM can measure high-level campaigns if they are discrete (broad ones that run for a set duration)\nGenerally our clients run several different campaigns at once; if we tried to measure that level of granularity the model would fail due to multicollinearity.  When this happens the model cannot estimate which variable drove a given outcome because they have the same pattern.  We aggregate data up to avoid this challenge, making other tools like Attribution better for campaign results \n\n--- SLIDE 88 ---\n\nTwo CPG studies by IRI (now Circana) in the past two decades estimated long-term media effects, especially upper funnel.  Both came up with roughly the same 1.8x estimate.\nIn the past five years we’ve seen these numbers validated in pharma, home-improvement and in non-profit.  \nThe IRI study also mentions price elasticity, which is another area where you can test the effects of changes in price / value perception and willingness to trade up as you change messaging.\nRule of Thumb LT ROI = 1.8x ST ROI\n\n--- SLIDE 89 ---\n\nMarketing Spend Effectiveness Toolbox\n\n--- SLIDE 90 ---\n\nSample Readout\n\n--- SLIDE 91 ---\n\nSample price elasticity decline driven by too high promo pressure\u000bIncreased trade promo pressure has negative effect on price elasticities\nIllustrative\n\n--- SLIDE 92 ---\n\nSample Growth Driver Analytics deliverable\u000bDrivers of Change in YoY total Volume Sales\nIllustrative\n\n--- SLIDE 93 ---\n\nSample Growth Driver Analytics deliverable\u000bBase and Incremental Volume Decomposition\nIllustrative\n\n--- SLIDE 94 ---\n\nSample Growth Driver Analytics deliverable\u000bPromotions damaging brand price elasticity. steering what happens next—faster, with clearer tradeoffs and higher confidence. Every enterprise is running a \"customer economy\" in real time: marketing spend, offers, pricing, digital experiences, service operations, loyalty programs, and retention motions. Those investments happen continuously—and they compound. Yet most organizations still operate measurement as a retrospective function: dashboards, readouts, and reconciliation cycles that arrive after the business has already moved. The winners will be the companies that can steer, not just see.\n\n--- SLIDE 60 ---\n\nFragmentation isn't the problem—it's the symptom. The deeper issue: the business can't see cross-journey tradeoffs fast enough to stop value from leaking. Most companies don't have a single \"measurement problem.\" They have a system problem: marketing, product, service, and finance are tightly coupled, but measurement is still handled in slices.\nAcquisition Without Churn Visibility\nA team can optimize acquisition efficiency without seeing downstream churn—winning the quarter while eroding the cohort.\nConversion Without Returns Context\nProduct can improve conversion rates without understanding the returns, contacts, and cost-to-serve that follow.\nEfficiency Without Loyalty Tradeoffs\nService can reduce handle time while quietly increasing churn risk—optimizing one metric while undermining another.\nThis creates tradeoff blindness: the inability to quantify what improves one outcome while quietly degrading another. Over time, this becomes a compounding tax on growth—wasted spend, missed upside, declining customer understanding, and a leadership culture that trusts intuition more than evidence because evidence arrives too late or arrives in conflict.\nThe Real Problem: \u000bValue Leakage in a System You Can't Fully See\n\n--- SLIDE 61 ---\n\nThe Measurement Situation\nIn the process of generating insights, recommendation & making decisions, majority of the time goes in wrangling data, switching between dashboards, KPIs, Metrics, Models and then arriving at half baked decisions which most of the time don’t create impact.  \n      25 %\n     35 %\n40 %\nData\nWork\nBrain Work\nDecision \nMaking \nWe are running a multi-billion-dollar customer economy without an operating system that can see it as a system.\nData from multiple sources, format, & structure often tends to take a lot of time to make it consumption ready.\nDashboards & Reports can get overwhelming with a range of KPIs & Metrics adds confusion.   \nDecisions become harder to get at, often tends to create less or no impact. Delays in decision making often leads to missed opportunity. \n\n--- SLIDE 62 ---\n\nOpportunity Which Clarity Taps On\n      25 %\n     35 %\n40 %\nData\nWork\nBrain Work\nDecision \nMaking \n(Human’s Work Faster) \nVALUE unlocked by CLARITY Agents\nMoving the enterprise from retrospective reporting to continuous, agentic decisioning.\nWe have an opportunity to create a framework of measurement which is composable and intelligent with AI, having the potential to create tangible value. \nComposable Data & Unified Context Leverage modern cloud platforms to create a shared, modular layer of definitions without rebuilding.\nAgentic Reasoning & Explanation Reason across contexts and detect uncertainty. The system gets smarter, the organization gets faster, and confidence compounds.\nThe Steering Loop:\nObserve → Explain → Simulate → Steer → Learn\nClarity operationalizes measurement as a closed loop—not a sequence of one-off analyses. Learning means:\nKeeping a governed record of what was recommended and why, preserving institutional reasoning\nTracking what actions were actually taken by operators and leadership teams\nMeasuring what happened after each decision—including downstream second-order effects\nImproving future guidance based on observed outcomes, not recalibrated assumptions\nEach cycle makes the next one faster, more accurate, and more trusted—turning measurement into a strategic asset that appreciates rather than a cost center that depreciates.\n\n--- SLIDE 65 ---\n\nModular Structure Makes Clarity Unique\nTranslation of Clarity Framework Into Technical Solution\nPlug-and-Play Components—Swap Data, Add Agents, Extend Widgets, Tailor Personas.\n\n--- SLIDE 66 ---\n\nWhy this is already real inside Blend\nClarity is not a future-state concept. Notes may be scrawled in handwriting, invoices come from multiple countries like Germany and Malysia, every law firm provides a different table format and could even vary between the clerks that prepared it. \nExisting tools for processing documents either require hundreds or thousands of detailed, labeled examples or the documents are highly structured.\nSolution Provided \nThe flexibility of large language models provides a new, powerful tool for document processing. \nLarge language models (LLMs), however, have the power to use contextual clues, in context learning, agentic reflection, and complex reasoning to deduce the meaning of the data extracted from PDFs and then restructure it into a formatted file. We leveraged this power to come up with a solution in a very limited amount of time with a very limited set of training examples. \nOur solution showcases the power of large language models for document processing. With only 40-50 training examples, we achieved near-perfect accuracy on test invoices, a tiny fraction of the data required by traditional AI models. \nEmployed novel techniques such as:\nHierarchical prompt chains to handle different invoice patterns \nFew-shot learning to quickly adapt to new formats\nPage-chucking with overlaps and memory for multi-page processing \nA serverless architecture for seamless integration and scalability \n\n--- SLIDE 117 ---\n\nGenAI Investment Assistant for Leading Investment Firm\nChallenges\nSignificant inefficiencies in extracting, analyzing, and revising The solution is being productionised for deployment by staff with a slick front-end use interface and the expectation is that the rollout will deliver significant cost reductions and increased employee engagement.\nThe pandemic drastically changed working patterns with many employees now returning to the office but on a hybrid basis. Our client wanted to optimise employee engagement and working patterns while strategically streamlining workplace locations to reduce costs. \nOur client: A leading global retailer and healthcare provider.\nWORKPLACE OPTIMISATION\n\n--- SLIDE 2 ---\n\nCHALLENGE\nSOLUTION\nOUTCOME\nWe developed a computer vision model to assess crop health by analysing image data from the growth towers, and to flag crops that do not grow as expected.     \nThe growth monitoring model has achieved over 75% accuracy and allows for the monitoring of crop health to be carried out remotely and automatically. Furthermore, the model is fully scalable and can be used to develop computer vision for any type of crop, allowing the system to be implemented across all growth towers.\nGrowth trays in vertical farming towers can be stacked up to 12 meters high, making it time-consuming to manually identify unhealthy plants to maximise yields and make the best use of resources.\nOur client: A global leader in vertical farming.\nREMOTE MONITORING \nOF CROPS\n\n--- SLIDE 3 ---\n\nManagers can now easily access insights on variances between planned and actual performance.  This gives them the tools to investigate why disparities happen and then take action to rectify this which not only means an improvement in estimated production times but a chance at increasing efficiency and thereby profit.\nCHALLENGE\nSOLUTION\nOUTCOME\nWe joined up key data sources to create a consolidated data asset and leveraged PaaS tools on Azure to ensure automation and rapid implementation. We then created an interactive dashboard to allow the client to extract actionable insight for use on the shop floor.\nOn the production floor, time is money. By having a view on the accuracy of production times and what impacts them, our client can modify their processes to maximise production. While data on both estimated and actual production times are collected, a combined view would be required to drive improvement and efficiency.\nOur client: An international lighting business.\n\nFACTORY PERFORMANCE INSIGHTS\n\n--- SLIDE 4 ---\n\nPartnering to establish a digital capability\n\nA UK oil & gas company\n\nCHALLENGE\nOur client was two years into a digital transformation journey, including developing an on-premise data warehouse. Our client saw a significant opportunity to prioritise a data first strategy by optimising and automating this process, thereby removing dependencies on SME knowledge, creating operational efficiencies throughout the planning process and increasing their fleet’s utilisation whilst reducing their carbon footprint.\n\n\n\nWHAT WE DID\nTo enable the automation of job allocations, we started by improving the client’s cloud infrastructure and enhancing their data through the deployment of Databricks, alongside tackling a series of ‘Quick Wins’. Updated metrics were integrated into the client’s suite of logistics management applications.\nThis was followed by the build of a semi-automated load management optimisation solution. The optimiser was built in such a way as to minimise the number of trailers required to transport all required items on a given day, consequently maximising fleet efficiency. By pre-processing the data for a given day in line with the constraints of the problem, it was possible to reduce both the time taken and the resources required to run the optimiser.\n\n\n\nRESULTS\nThe client now has improved key metrics available (e.g., trailer utilisation metrics), and the enhanced architecture has enabled the build of the optimisation solution as well as the ability to better exploit and manipulate their existing data.\n\n\nPeterson 1\nAn Energy Logistics Company\n\n--- SLIDE 7 ---\n\nThe client now has easy access to view and utilise their data in the BI Dashboard and the enhanced architecture means we can now start automating their allocation processes to increase productivity and lower costs.\nCHALLENGE\nSOLUTION\nOUTCOME\nTo enable the automation of job allocations, we started by improving the client’s cloud infrastructure and enhancing their data through the deployment of Databricks. This section to be completed by C2G Corporate:\nSection II. This section to be completed by C2G Consultant:\nExecutive Summary:  What is/was the business issue? \n[C2G: Cut/paste from the signed SOW or proposal, if applicable.]\n[Consultant: Please edit as necessary]\nThe client wanted a resource that will be responsible for managing the strategy, execution and analytical requirements within the balance transfer marketing group. \nPlease describe the role (include marketing channel).\nIn this role, I was to manage the strategy for Balcon program.  My focus was to work closely with internal Risk and Decision Management partners to develop and implement ways to deliver the best pricing offers and customer experience to Citi card members.  While leading the program, I introduced a new agency and worked on several pricing initiatives that would be executed through our team.  I also worked with channel partners (email, direct mail, digital, mobile and phone) to forecast balance transfer $ volume and revenue goals, as well as, provide actuals for each campaign as data and metrics came available.\nDeliverables: \n[C2G: Cut/paste from the signed SOW or proposal, if applicable.]\nThe deliverables were more of a non-traditional tangible assets, it was more of more efficiency and streamlining processes.\nDevelopment of new campaigns\nWorking with execution and creatives partners on my team, I would roadmap out the entire year of tests and pricing initiatives we wanted to run within the campaign.  Usually providing targeting elements and hypotheses of outcomes and behaviors.\nLeveraging analytics and data science expertise to drive decisions across campaigns\nDue to the long nature of our campaigns, 6 months of planning and 3 months of post offer, our metrics would not be able to affect the next few months of work. Also we were not very agile when it came to the execution process.  However, we did take our learnings and applied them to future campaigns, which we put on our roadmap.\nDevelopment of communication to socialize performance\nI created monthly meetings to review Balcon Strategy for a team of over 60 members.  In these meetings I would walk through our upcoming tests, previous performances and any initiatives that were close to being implemented so all of our team members who work directly or in-directly on Balcon could learn what we are doing and what our results were.  This hopefully helped everyone gain some pride in their work and what they did mattered.  We also had a few quarterly review sessions that the product teams were involved with.\nStrong collaboration with execution channel partners (Creative Management, Production, Decision Management, RISK, Database Marketing, etc.) to ensure campaign integrity and success.\nI made sure to always involve my partners in whatever I was doing.  This not only gave me support, but sometimes brought up tests in the past that were tried or started but never finished. I was able to learn from those early versions and develop tests on top of them.  Plus, when I didn’t know where to go for answers, these partners were truly helpful in getting me the info or guiding me to the right place.  For some of the pricing tests I was looking to launch, I relied heavily on DM and Risk because without the knowledge of sizing and potential impact to our program (revenue and transfer $ volume), we could be testing to gain nothing or lose even more.  \nObservations:  [Consultant: Please complete.]\nHow do/did you add value to the project?  How do/did you help the client resolve their issue(s)?\nI believe I added value to the project in a few different ways.  One way is I was coming in with fresh eyes which helped others who have been working in Balcon for years, to see a new perspective. I was able to challenge their thinking and ways of working in the process (in a good way).  As I heard from some, I was a breath a fresh air, and really could see more than a single way to do things.  My value was shown by understanding not only the financial side of Balcon, but the creative and execution side.  This provided all to view the program holistically vs their silo, even across departments.  By me being able to speak to numerous levels of the program, I could help resolve issues faster, since I didn’t always have to ask around for help.  \nWhat skills or experience do/did you bring to this project to make it successful?\nMy experience of leading teams, without direct reports, has helped me in this role as I had to cross many departments in different levels of the company. Please quantify or simply speak to the ROI…\n\tIn 2018 we had a plan of $8.7B of transfer volume, but early in the year we had a reduction of budget which affected marketing dollars and population sizes. We overcame this and had a new goal of $7.1B in transfer volume and revenue of $126MM.  We were also under a transfer cap of $600M for 2018.  In 2019 we raised the cap to $650MM but then once the Federal Reserve said it would pause any rate hikes we decided to uncap balance transfers and in April we lifted the cap to unconstrained. Our 2019 goal is $9.9B in transfer volume and $139MM in revenue.\nWhat systems or databases do/did you use?  \nI used a few Citi created programs and some reporting tools like Site Catalyst, Tableau, IBM Cognos and others. Attach any documents here.\nI have recommended that some of the pricing initiatives be paused or on hold due to effort and capacity, as well as, proposed test is not going to happen in that manner, and should be reworked.\nWhat additional information can you provide that sums up this project? \nWhat do/did you like or not like about this project…what are/were your pain points?\n\tThis project has been intense. critical in the highly regulated financial sector - this initiative aimed to enable analysts to focus on deeper insights and strategic decision-making.\nThrough the development of an AI Transformation and Adoption Framework, Blend ensured that AI solutions were explainable, scalable, and designed to meet Franklin Templeton's rigorous operational and compliance standards.\nThe solution integrated advanced AI techniques including advanced retrieval-augmented generation, AI agents, embedding algorithms, vector stores for semantic understanding, and prompt optimization to align with analysts' specific writing styles.\nImplemented comprehensive data integration pipelines connecting proprietary internal files, public financial filings, and third-party vendor data, with built-in explainability features for trust and adoption.\nDeveloped a modular, scalable architecture enabling seamless expansion to other groups and subsidiaries within Franklin Templeton's ecosystem.\n\nOutcomes:\nSuccessfully established trust and adoption through explainability features, creating a foundation for confidence in AI-driven processes across the organization.\nSolution became a cornerstone of Franklin Templeton's AI transformation journey, with planned expansion to support additional use cases including risk management and client-facing advisory tools.\n\n\n\nCreated a replicable model for AI-driven transformation in financial services, demonstrating Blend's vertical expertise and ability to deliver enterprise-scale solutions in the investment management space.\nForecasted 80-90% reduction in time required for drafting investment recommendations, allowing analysts to focus on deeper research and strategic initiatives. This new feature is currently being rolled out and scaled across the team. \n\nRelevant criteria:\nVertical competencies and expertise (Financial Services)\n*Blend & Client Highly Confidential. Data Warehousing\n4.1 ELT (Extract Load Transform) \n\nTo automate the daily upload of the flat files, Databricks Auto Loader can be leveraged to incrementally and efficiently process new data files. Auto Loader provides automatic schema inference and evolution and incrementally processes new files as they arrive in cloud object storage. Auto Loader also automatically scales compute infrastructure for cost savings and it provides monitoring via metrics in the event log. Databricks also allows you to bring your data into the platform with high efficiency using a growing number of native ingestion connectors for analytics. Databricks supports star schemas and leverages Delta lake to create the fact and dimension tables. When you build your star schema with Databricks SQL, Delta Lake, is leveraged to enable ACID transactions, time travel, indexing and caching amongst other benefits.\n\n4.2 Schema Design\nA commonly used design pattern for Databricks is a Medallion (or ‘multi-hop’)  architecture which is used to logically organize data in a lakehouse, with the goal of incrementally and progressively improving the structure and quality of data as it flows through each layer of the architecture (from Bronze ⇒ Silver ⇒ Gold layer tables). Some benefits of this architecture include a simple data model which is  easy to understand and implement, it enables incremental ETL and you can recreate your tables from raw data at any time.\n\n Databricks stores tables in Delta format which is an open-source table format. Delta Lake has simple to uses features such as Liquid Clustering, which is an innovative data management technique that replaces table partitioning and ZORDER, so you no longer have to fine-tune your data layout to achieve optimal query performance. Delta Lake UniForm is a feature of Delta Lake which enables Apache Iceberg reader clients to read Delta Tables. Databricks also recently acquired Tabular, founded by the original creators of Apache IceBerg, to lead the way with data compatibility so that you are no longer limited by which lakehouse format your data is in.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n14\n\n--- SLIDE 15 ---\n\n\nTechnical Requirements: \n5. Security and Compliance  \n6.1 Data Security\n1. Encryption\nYes, Databricks can meet the requirement of encrypting all data, both in transit and at rest, using industry-standard encryption protocols.\nFor data at rest, Databricks supports adding a customer-managed key to help protect and control access to data. This includes managed services data in the Databricks control plane and data on the Amazon S3 bucket in your AWS account that you specified when you created your workspace. Databricks also supports encrypting data in S3 using server-side encryption.\nFor data in transit, user queries and transformations are typically sent to your clusters over an encrypted channel. However, if your environment requires that data be encrypted at all times, you can create an init script that configures your clusters to encrypt traffic between worker nodes, using AES 128-bit encryption over a TLS 1.2 connection.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n19\n\n--- SLIDE 20 ---\n\n\nTechnical Requirements: \n6. Security and Compliance  \n6.1 Data Security\n2. Access controls\nYes, Databricks can meet the requirement of implementing robust access control mechanisms, including role-based access control (RBAC) and multi-factor authentication (MFA).\nFor RBAC, Databricks provides different access control systems for different securable objects. This includes workspace-level securable objects, account-level securable objects, and data securable objects. Access control lists (ACLs) can be used to configure permission to access workspace objects such as notebooks and SQL Warehouses. Account role-based access control can be used to configure permission to use account-level objects such as service principals and groups. There are also built-in roles on the Azure Databricks platform, and users, service principals, and groups can be assigned these roles.\nIn addition to RBAC, Databricks also supports Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), and advanced techniques such as Row Filtering and Column Masking. These features provide fine-grained access management, allowing you to effectively manage data access and ensure compliance within your Databricks environments\nDatabricks can meet the Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) requirement across all cloud platforms. However, the specific method of implementation may vary depending on the cloud platform in use (More info can be provided on request) \n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n20\n\n--- SLIDE 21 ---\n\n\nTechnical Requirements: \n6. Audit trails and logging\nYes, Databricks does meet this requirement. Databricks has a system in place that emits Audit Logs by calling one of the provided Scala methods that write logs to an audit.json file on each pod. These logs are then delivered to customers within 15 minutes.\nThe audit logs record events related to security, such as changed authentication methods, user logins, changed cluster instance profiles or notebook ACLs. They also log any user action involving modifying state (e.g., creating a cluster, running a job, or deleting a notebook) and any user action involving reading customer data (e.g., tables, files). Actions that help to trace or debug system state over time, like renaming a Databricks notebook, are also logged.\nThe logs are designed to provide sufficient detail to identify who accessed the data or source code, what changes were made, and when these events occurred. However, it's important to note that passwords or tokens are not emitted as part of audit logs to ensure security.\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n\n21\n\n--- SLIDE 22 ---\n\n\nTechnical Requirements: \n6. The team will provide everyday support, resolve issues, and answer FAQ’s.\n\nActivities:\nLogging tickets\nUser Education\nNew users\nTriaging and resolving tickets\nImplementation of minor changes\n\nThis role would typically be filled by a Data Engineer\n\nSecond Line Support\n\n2nd line support will solve more complex issues and requests. This could include data hashing and anonymisation.\n\nAccess Control: Unity Catalog will manage access to PII, ensuring that only authorised individuals with a genuine business need can view the data.\n\nAudit Logging: Databricks’ Unity Catalog provides an audit log table to track table access, user activity, and permission changes, featuring a clear schema for event coverage.\n\nComprehensive Coverage: The audit log table captures a wide range of actions across Databricks accounts and workspaces, aiding in thorough data management and compliance tracking.\nThe solution which is required for ensuring security and compliance standards are always met. Adhering to regulatory requirements and taking reasonable measures to ensure the privacy of Barb’s panellists and subscribers are respected. To do this, GDPR compliance will be in place by implementing a right-to-be-forgotten feature, managing PII through hashing and anonymisation, and using Unity Catalog for access control and auditing. Unity Catalog provides detailed audit logs for tracking data access and user activity. This will provide comprehensive audit trails and logging to track all access and modifications to data and source code, allowing you to identify who accessed the data and source code and when changes were made, via the Barb DataHub. The tools and strategies to the right, show how the 6.2 compliance requirements are met. \n\n6.1 of Data security can be seen through the access control available in Unity Catalog, which Databricks and either AWS/Azure storage will provide  via encryption on all data. \n\n--- SLIDE 45 ---\n\n\n\n\nDatabricks will serve as the backbone of the solution, providing centralised access control/data Structure: Centralized (Orchestrator-Driven)\n\nArchitecture\nBenefits (Pros)\nDrawbacks (Cons)\nSAS (Single Agent Loop)\nSimple architecture\nEasy to debug & maintain\nLow overhead\nLimited scalability\nSingle point of failure\nNot for complex reasoning\nIndependent Agents\nHigh parallelism\nBuilt-in redundancy\nAgents evolve independently\nHigh coordination overhead\nRisk of conflicting outputs\nHard to enforce global optimization\nCentralized (Orchestrator-Driven)\nClear governance\nDeterministic execution\nEasier monitoring & debugging\nOrchestrator bottleneck\nSingle point of failure (if not hardened)\nScaling is complex\nDecentralized (Peer-to-Peer)\nNo single point of failure\nHighly scalable & resilient\nSuits distributed environments\nComplex coordination logic\nSlower decision-making\nHard to reason about global state\nHybrid (Central + Distributed)\nBalances control & scalability\nFlexible execution patterns\nStrong fault tolerance\nHighest design complexity\nDifficult to test & maintain\nRequires mature observability\nClear orchestration and decision authority\nPredictable, auditable multi-agent execution\nFaster debugging and controlled scaling\nEasily extensible to add new agents\nWhy we chose Centralized hub-spoke structure\n\n--- SLIDE 23 ---\n\nUI Framework: Streamlit\nCategory\nStreamlit\nNext.js\nBest Use Cases\nInternal tools, POCs, analytics dashboards, agent demos\nProduction-grade consumer apps, complex UIs, high-performance systems\nPython Agent Integration\nNative, seamless (same Python runtime)\nRequires API backend to connect to Python agents\nDeployment Complexity\nVery easy (Streamlit Cloud, Docker, internal servers)\nRequires production-grade front-end deployment + backend services\nUI Flexibility\nModerate (prebuilt components, limited styling)\nVery High (fully customizable React components)\nPerformance Profile\nGood for dashboards and data apps\nExcellent for large-scale, highly interactive web apps\nCVS Action Center Fit\n⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Ideal for POC phase\n⭐⭐☆☆☆ Too heavy for current needs\nFastest path to value for POC: Streamlit enables rapid development of analytics dashboards and agent demos with minimal engineering overhead—ideal for validating the multi-agent Action Center quickly.\nNative Python + agent integration: Seamless integration with Python-based agents, orchestration logic, and Snowflake queries—no additional API or front-end layers required.\nConsistency with existing CVS tools: Several existing CVS internal tools and analytics applications are already built using Streamlit, reducing adoption friction and aligning with established development patterns.\nRight tool for current phase: Provides sufficient UI capabilities for internal users and decision-making workflows today, while leaving the option open to migrate to Next.js for a future production-grade experience if needed\n\n--- SLIDE 24 ---\n\nAgent Framework Selection: LangGraph for POC\nLangGraph\nGraph-based orchestration with deterministic flows and state management. Ideal for complex, multi-step supply chain workflows requiring full control and predictability.\nGoogle ADK\nAdvanced planning framework with automated evaluation capabilities. Strong for autonomous agents but less control over execution paths.\nAutoGen\nConversation-based multi-agent collaboration. Flexible dialogue patterns but potentially non-deterministic behavior in production environments.\nCrewAI\nLightweight framework optimized for rapid prototyping. Fast iteration cycles but may lack enterprise-grade features for scale.\nDeterministic and controllable orchestration: LangGraph’s graph-based execution ensures predictable, auditable agent behavior—critical for supply-chain analytics and business trust.\nDesigned for complex multi-agent workflows: Natively supports a central orchestrator coordinating multiple specialist agents with clear state management and parallel/sequential execution.\nFast to deliver, production-oriented by design: Provides strong control and reliability without sacrificing development speed, making it ideal for a POC that must scale toward production.\nBest balance among alternatives: Offers more execution control than Google ADK and AutoGen, while being more enterprise-ready and predictable than lightweight frameworks like CrewAI.\nAzure AI Foundry\n\n--- SLIDE 25 ---\n\nObservability & Evaluation Tools\nArize Phoenix\nCategory: LLM Observability + Tracing + Evaluation\nStrengths: Deep step-level traces • Detects hallucinations & grounding errors • Visual debugging of multi-agent workflows\nBest For: Debugging agent reasoning, evaluating correctness\nLangSmith\nCategory: Experiment & Trace Tracking\nStrengths: LangChain/LangGraph integration • Prompt versioning • A/B testing • Failure monitoring\nBest For: Prompt testing, orchestrator debugging, regression testing\nGoogle ADK Evaluators\nCategory: Agent Evaluation + Trajectory Checking\nStrengths: Tool sequencing validation • Action trajectory verification • Ground-truth datasets\nBest For: Formal agent evaluation, verifying multi-step decisions\nDeep agent-reasoning visibility: Phoenix provides step-level, semantic observability into multi-agent reasoning, making it ideal for debugging correctness, grounding, and hallucinations in complex workflows.\nDesigned for LLM and agent evaluation: Built specifically for LLM systems, Phoenix goes beyond system metrics to evaluate reasoning quality and decision accuracy—critical for supply-chain agent trust.\nPerfect fit for early validation: Enables rapid identification of failure modes and reasoning gaps during the POC, accelerating iteration before scaling to formal ground-truth and production monitoring.\nAzure AI Foundry\n\n--- SLIDE 26 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE 27 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE 28 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE 29 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE 30 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE By classifying upfront, the solution saves significant processing overhead and latency, optimizing performance.\nA toxicity and safety filter screens for inappropriate or offensive entries, ensuring the system does not return results for queries containing abusive, hateful, or derogatory input. Tolerances for this model are configurable in total and discretely for six different types of toxicity.\nA named-entity recognition system extracts property details in the search. This can include amenities on property, such as a spa or private beach. It also recognizes attractions such as sporting events, museums or theatres. It enables intuitive filtering by price, such as “less than $400” in multiple currencies, including award points. \n\nA large language model (Google Gemini) is used to retrieve relevant world knowledge when a guest searches for new topics not stored in the enriched catalog. This includes general knowledge unrelated to specific hotels. If the guest wants to go white water rafting, the LLM will respond with the top places in the world to do that.\nAssess\nEnvision\nImplement\nActivate\nA catalog enrichment process to cache knowledge built up from authored and user-generated content as well as past search results. This process improves the performance of future queries by providing relevant entity matches. Process includes human in the loop review to prevent hallucinations from entering catalog.\nOptimize\nHow it works\nBlend developed several AI-based capabilities to enable personalized, intent-based property recommendations.\nClassification\nSafety\nRecognition\nComprehension\nMemory\nSimple destination queries with no additional parameters route to existing flow saving compute\nComplex queries with features, amenities, experience use only entity extraction for low latency\nEntirely new knowledge queries (e.g., “white water rafting”) utilize the full stack of capabilities\nSystematic catalog improvements increase effectiveness of entity search\nPrivate & Confidential\n\n--- SLIDE 5 ---\n\nHow the solution understands a query\nClassification\nHotels in Phoenix with swimming and tesla charging under $400\nIntent\nDestination\nAmenity\nPool\nAmenity\nEV Charger\nPrice\n< 400 USD\n1\nClassification\nAlpine ski resort for romantic honeymoon with nightclubs and spa\nIntent\nStyle\n2\nRomantic\nPhoenix\nType\nResort\nAmenity\nSpa\nAttraction\nNightclub\nActivity\nAlpine Skiing\n Listed Amenity\n Listed Amenity\n In Catalog\n In Catalog\n Listed\n Listed\n Unknown\nLLM Call\nFind top global destinations for Alpine Skiing\nLLM Destination Response\nFrench Alps: Three Valleys; Chamonix; Courchevel\nSwiss Alps: Zermatt; Verbier; St. Mortitz\nAustrian Alps: St Anton am Alrberg; Kitzbühel; Ischgl\nItalian Alps: Cortina d’Ampezzo; Madonna di Campiglio; Cervinia\nPrivate & Confidential\nSafe\nSafe\n\n--- SLIDE 6 ---\n\nSynthetic Training Data\nNo prior history data was available for training and tuning models.       "raw_text": "Lead Qualification Questions\nAgentic Data Platform\nTechnical Discovery Guide for Partners\nIntroduction\nThis guide provides technical discovery questions to help you understand a prospect's current data infrastructure and operational challenges. It's organized into two categories:\n• Top 5-7 Qualifying Questions: Start here. These rapid-fire questions reveal whether the prospect has the core pain points we solve.\n• More Questions to Ask: Deeper technical exploration for when you've identified a qualified lead and want to understand their architecture in detail.\nUse the qualifying questions first to assess fit quickly. If they answer 3+ in ways that suggest operational pain, move to the deeper questions to understand scope and complexity. These questions are best asked when speaking with CTOs, VPs of Data Engineering, Data Architects, or Infrastructure teams.\nRemember: Listen more than you talk. Let technical leaders tell their story. Your sales team handles budget, timeline, and deal progression.\nPart 1: Top Qualifying Questions\nAsk these first. If 3 or more answers reveal operational pain, you have a qualified lead. If not, keep them warm and circle back in 6 months.\nQ1: Walk me through your data stack. What are you running for warehousing, lakes, and data processing?\nWhy it matters: Reveals whether they're cloud-native or legacy. Cloud stacks are easier to integrate. Fragmented stacks = pain.\n→ Are these cloud or on-prem?\n→ How are these systems connected? Do they share metadata?\n→ Who owns integration between them?\nQ2: How often do your data pipelines fail, and when they do, how long does it take to fix them?\nWhy it matters: Frequent failures + long MTTR = core pain point. Reveals operational maturity and whether they're reactive or proactive.\n→ What causes most failures? (Schema, infrastructure, data quality?)\n→ Do you detect failures automatically, or do users tell you?\n→ What's your typical time-to-resolution for critical issues?\nQ3: Tell me about data onboarding. When you need a new data source, how long does it take from request to available for analysis?\nWhy it matters: 4-8 weeks = bottleneck. Quick turnaround = mature infrastructure. This directly impacts AI project velocity.\n→ Who's involved in the onboarding process?\n→ What are the blocking steps?\n→ Is it engineer-driven or self-service?\nQ4: How many AI or ML projects are you running, and what percentage have made it to production?\nWhy it matters: <50% success rate = data or governance is blocking. This is the biggest business pain.\n→ What's slowing down the pilots that haven't reached production?\n→ Is it data quality, data freshness, or governance friction?\n→ How long does it take to move from pilot to production?\nQ5: What percentage of your data team's time is spent on routine operations (firefighting, monitoring, fixing) vs. strategic work?\nWhy it matters: 60-80% ops = burnout and frustration. This metric signals whether they have the pain motivation to change.\n→ If operations were automated, what would your team build instead?\n→ Is team turnover a concern?\n→ Can they even think about innovation, or are they too busy?\nQ6: When bad data reaches production (analytics or AI), how do you find out, and how long does it take to trace and fix?\nWhy it matters: User complaints + slow root-cause = reactive culture. Automated detection + fast response = mature culture.\n→ Who discovers bad data issues?\n→ Can you trace data lineage from impact back to source?\n→ Do you have automated quality tests?\nQ7: How are you handling data governance and compliance today? Is it mostly manual or automated?\nWhy it matters: Manual governance = audit friction and slow change. This reveals compliance risk and risk appetite for transformation.\n→ How long do audit cycles take?\n→ Do you have automated enforcement, or is it policy + manual checks?\n→ How quickly can you make a governance change?\nPart 2: More Questions to Ask\nOnce you've qualified the lead with Part 1, use these questions to understand architecture depth, scope, and implementation complexity. These are organized by topic area.\nInfrastructure & Architecture\nQ8: How are your data warehouse, data lake, and other data systems connected? Do they share metadata or schemas?\nWhy it matters: Fragmented systems mean manual integration work. Understanding connections reveals orchestration needs.\n→ Are integrations manual or automated?\n→ Do business users see a single view of truth?\n→ Who manages each system?\nQ9: What's your current approach to real-time vs. batch data ingestion? How do you handle streaming or event-driven data?\nWhy it matters: Batch-only systems can't support modern AI. Understanding this reveals infrastructure gaps.\n→ What percentage of your data is real-time vs. batch?\n→ Do you have streaming infrastructure (Kafka, Kinesis)?\n→ How fresh does your AI model data need to be?\n→ What's preventing real-time at scale?\nQ10: How are you currently handling unstructured data (text, images, logs, PDFs)? Where does it live, and how do you connect it to structured data?\nWhy it matters: Unstructured data is typically siloed. Understanding integration reveals scope of platform need.\n→ What types of unstructured data do you have?\n→ Where is it stored?\n→ Have you tried to use it for analytics or AI? What was hard?\n→ Do you have full-text or semantic search?\nQ11: Tell me about your data catalog or metadata management. How do teams discover data and understand lineage?\nWhy it matters: Poor metadata = tribal knowledge, slow onboarding, governance gaps. Understanding maturity reveals need for semantic layer.\n→ Do you have a formal data catalog tool?\n→ How current and trustworthy is your metadata?\n→ Can you trace data lineage from source to business metric?\n→ Do business users actually use your catalog?\nPipeline & Data Quality Operations\nQ12: Schema changes are notoriously painful. How do you handle schema evolution when source systems change?\nWhy it matters: Manual schema management = bottleneck. Understanding this reveals automation need.\n→ How often do schema changes cause downstream failures?\n→ Who detects schema drift, and when?\n→ What's the process to update schemas?\n→ Have you had incidents where schema changes broke production?\nQ13: How do you currently detect data quality issues? Do you have monitoring, validation rules, or quality metrics?\nWhy it matters: Manual/reactive detection = pain. Proactive detection = maturity. Understanding this shows governance infrastructure gaps.\n→ Do you catch quality issues before or after they impact users?\n→ Who owns data quality?\n→ Do you have automated testing for critical datasets?\n→ What's your biggest data quality challenge right now?\nQ14: When a data pipeline fails or has quality issues, what's the debugging process? How long does root-cause analysis take?\nWhy it matters: Slow debugging = operational toil. Fast debugging = mature infrastructure.\n→ Can you see logs and metrics across your entire data stack?\n→ Do you have centralized observability, or do you check multiple systems?\n→ How much of the debugging is manual vs. automated?\nQ15: Do you have data quality SLAs (Service Level Agreements) for critical data?\nWhy it matters: Explicit SLAs = mature. No SLAs = expectations are vague.\n→ What are your freshness, completeness, accuracy SLAs?\n→ How are they tracked and monitored?\n→ What happens when SLAs are breached?\n→ Are SLAs defined for all data or just critical datasets?\nGovernance & Compliance\nQ16: Walk me through your current data governance structure. Who owns access control, data ownership, and compliance?\nWhy it matters: Governance scattered across teams = inconsistent rules. Centralized = scalable.\n→ Is governance CDO-led or distributed?\n→ How do you manage access control and PII/sensitive data?\n→ How long does it take to make a governance change?\n→ Do you have automated enforcement?\nQ17: How consistent is your data across different systems? Do you reconcile data between your warehouse, lake, and operational systems?\nWhy it matters: Multiple systems = multiple versions of truth. Reconciliation reveals data consistency maturity.\n→ How often do you find discrepancies?\n→ Who investigates and fixes them?\n→ Do users trust your 'single source of truth'?\n→ How much manual reconciliation happens?\nAI & Real-Time Data\nQ18: Do you have a feature store, or are ML features currently built by hand for each model?\nWhy it matters: Manual feature engineering = slow, duplicated work. Feature store maturity reveals ML infrastructure gaps.\n→ How are ML training features generated?\n→ Do features get reused across models?\n→ How long does it take to engineer a new feature?\n→ Is feature freshness an issue?\nQ19: How many of your AI models require real-time data vs. batch? What's preventing you from going more real-time?\nWhy it matters: Real-time requirements = need for streaming infrastructure. Understanding latency needs reveals scope.\n→ What's your latency tolerance for model features?\n→ Do you have streaming infrastructure?\n→ Is latency a blocker for any AI initiatives?\n→ What would you build if latency weren't a constraint?\nTeam & Execution\nQ20: Walk me through how your data team is structured. How many people, what roles, and how is work allocated?\nWhy it matters: Team structure reveals whether issues are organizational or tooling. Understanding allocation shows whether they can execute.\n→ Data engineers vs. analytics engineers vs. scientists—what's the split?\n→ Are teams centralized or distributed across business units?\n→ What's the engineer-to-stakeholder ratio?\n→ How is work prioritized and allocated?\nQ21: How mature is your infrastructure-as-code and deployment practices? Can engineers deploy changes safely and quickly?\nWhy it matters: Manual deployments = slow, risky. IaC + CI/CD = fast, reliable. This reveals execution capability.\n→ Do you use IaC for data infrastructure?\n→ Do you have CI/CD pipelines for data code?\n→ What's your deployment cycle for pipeline changes?\n→ How often do deployments cause incidents?\nQ22: Tell me about query performance and optimization. Are slow queries a problem?\nWhy it matters: Slow queries = BI adoption friction and AI training delays. Understanding this reveals infrastructure bottlenecks.\n→ Do you have visibility into slow queries?\n→ How do you prioritize query optimization?\n→ Is it reactive or proactive tuning?\n→ Who owns query optimization?",

      "raw_text": "\n--- SLIDE 1 ---\n\nOCS Anomaly Detection AI Architectural Review\n5 February 2026\n\n--- SLIDE 2 ---\n\nAgenda\nDesign Principles & Requirements\nCost Overview\nMethodology Overview with Diagrams\nDesign Dependencies \n04\n05\n01\n02\nData Security & Privacy\nUpcoming Milestones\n06\n03\nReview proposed architecture and seek feedback ahead of technical design sign-off\nObjective\n\n--- SLIDE 3 ---\n\nProject Overview\n\n--- SLIDE 4 ---\n\nMain message criteria\n\n--- SLIDE 5 ---\n\n01 \u000bDesign Principles & Requirements \n\n--- SLIDE 6 ---\n\nDesign Principles\n\n--- SLIDE 7 ---\n\nExecution frequency: \u000bOne model run per site per operational day at 9am.\nOperational usage: \u000bOne supervisor per site receiving a single summarised message per working day.\nOperational days: \u000bInitial 3 sites don’t operate on weekends, so 5 runs per week. \u000bExpansion into sites that run 7 days a week will have insights delivered 7 days a week.\nEnvironments: \u000bThere will be DEV, UAT and PROD environments, connected to the associated OCX environment. Once running, PROD will be the only environment that is \"switched on\" (i.e. schedule is enabled). DEV and UAT will be disabled to reduce costs, but will be in a state to be re-enabled in the case of development or testing.\nIf OCX Prod Pipeline has failed and there is no data available for the previous day, the Anomaly Detection will not attempt to send out messages to sites.\nAnomaly Detection system to be built in separate subscriptions from OCX, using VNet peering to connect to the OCX SQL Database, and utilising a separate Azure DevOps project to provide repositories, CI/CD, and documentation.\nNotifications: Anomaly detection system failures will be raised via Application Insights to a designated list of OCS email accounts. Notification of other types (e.g. pipeline did not run due to lack of data availability) also to be configured through AppInsights. \nRequirements\nAssumptions\n\n--- SLIDE 8 ---\n\n02 \u000bMethodology Overview with Diagrams\n\n--- SLIDE 9 ---\n\nData Flow\n1\nOrchestration, monitoring & audit: Azure-hosted functions orchestrate the pipeline, log run metadata and provide traceability.\n\nData acquisition: Client SQL data is ingested on a scheduled cadence\n\n\nData readiness: Schema and completeness checks are applied before processing so partial or missing data does not generate misleading outputs.\n\nAnomaly detection: A DS model performs all statistical analysis and produces structured anomaly signals, keeping reasoning explicit and testable.\n\nLLM summarisation: The LLM converts structured anomaly outputs into human-readable summaries only, reducing hallucination risk and limiting cost.\n\nDelivery & acknowledgment: After an anomaly is detected, a message with its details is sent to the MS Teams user group, where receivers can acknowledge the message with a button built into the message\n\nSecurity boundary: VNets and private endpoints to be used for data access and model inference to keep traffic within Azure and reduce exposure.\n3\n4\n5\n6\n2\n7\n2\n1\n3\n4\n5\n6\n7\n\n--- SLIDE 10 ---\n\nArchitecture Diagram\nAzure Functions chosen as the logic engine to enable scalability as the number of sites increases. They provide elastic compute and are ideal for scheduled daily tasks, with consumption costs returning to 0 once tasks are complete. \n\nA Virtual Network encompasses all infrastructure, with VNet Peering used to connect securely to the existing OCX Database\n\nPrivate Endpoint to connect to a network-isolated instance of Azure hosted OpenAI's GPT model\n\nLogic Apps used to send Teams messages and receive acknowledgments \n\nBlob Storage as a backend data store for the documents: anomaly output JSON files, LLM response text & Teams Adaptive Cards JSON files) \n\nApplication insights to access logs from the Azure Functions and send notifications to monitoring teams.\n\n1\n2\n3\n4\n5\n6\n1\n2\n3\n5\n6\n2\n\n--- SLIDE 11 ---\n\nAnomaly detection\u000bA combined statistical and rules-based approach is recommended to identify statistical anomalies while incorporating business context.\nOperationally grounded: Statistical deviations are only escalated when they also satisfy business rules (policy thresholds, data-quality gates, coverage constraints) to ensure alerts remain meaningful across both new and established sites.\nSite-aware by design: Baselines are computed per site using rolling baselines (e.g. 14/30 days), allowing the model to adapt to different operating patterns across LBS, B&Q, and OCS environments.\nMinimal training requirements: The approach avoids supervised labels and long training cycles, detecting normal behaviour from recent site activity and supporting phased site onboarding with the data currently available.\nLBS & OCS\n(Real data)\nB&Q\n(Synthetic data)\nIndicative model process per site\n\n--- SLIDE 12 ---\n\nLLM Model Selection\n*Assumes one run per day, one supervisor per site, LLM inference cost estimates do not include infrastructure costs\nAzure deployment: \nAzure Direct Models (OpenAI GPT) are selected so model hosting, management, and inference run entirely within Azure AI Foundry under Microsoft’s operational boundary, without introducing an external inference platform (e.g., Anthropic, Google).\nSecurity & data residency: \nFor Azure Direct Models, prompts and outputs remain within the OCS’s Azure tenant and geography, with no data used for model training or shared externally.\nFit-for-purpose LLM model: \nModels were evaluated on summarisation quality, latency, throughput, and cost; advanced reasoning capabilities are not required for this use case.\nCost & behaviour: \nGPT-5.1 avoids the unpredictable reasoning-token behaviour observed in GPT-5-mini while remaining cheaper than GPT-5.2.\nGPT-5.1 via Azure OpenAI is recommended as the LLM for this use case, providing the best balance of output quality, performance, cost predictability, and enterprise-grade security.\n\n--- SLIDE 13 ---\n\nEnd-to-end logging\nKey outputs are logged at each stage of the pipeline, including statistical scores and threshold evaluations from the anomaly detection model, as well as LLM-generated summaries and rationale for any recommendations.\n\nPersistent storage\nAll logged outputs are written to the data store incrementally. This ensures partial results are preserved even if downstream processing fails, enabling post-failure analysis, replay, and recovery without loss of diagnostic context.\n\nUser acknowledgement tracking\nThe system captures user acknowledgement when the message is received and read. This feedback is stored alongside model outputs, creating a closed audit loop between detection, recommendation, and human response.\nDeterministic detection layer\nAnomaly detection is handled by a DS model that produces quantitative, testable outputs with clear inputs and decision criteria. This keeps the core detection logic separate and allows model behaviour to be validated independently of how results are presented.\n\nLLM interpretation layer\nThe LLM is used to summarise results and explain outcomes, not to determine whether an anomaly exists. Separating explanation from decision-making reduces reliance on non-deterministic reasoning and limits hallucination risk.\nExplainability\nAuditability\nEnsuring AI outputs are auditable and explainable\nStoring all model outputs enables transparent auditing while using the LLM only for summarisation reduces hallucinations.\n\n--- SLIDE 14 ---\n\n03 \u000bData Security & Privacy\n\n--- SLIDE 15 ---\n\nVirtual Network: The Anomaly Detection system will have it's own VNet, which will be peered to the OCX VNet. Subnets for relevant component groups will be created, e.g., for private endpoints, logic apps, Azure Functions.\nNetwork Access: All infrastructure components will either only allow VNet traffic, or will be completely isolated and access via a private endpoint.\nNetwork Security Groups (for certain subnets) will be implemented to reduce access in-and outbound, especially for the Logic Apps to Teams connections\nManaged identities will be used to control the access between the infrastructure components within the Anomaly Detection subscription. A service principle is preferred for Database access to the OCX to reduce dependencies between subscriptions\nSecrets will be managed in a Key Vault within the VNet\nManaged Identity for the logic apps to be able to send teams messages\nNetworking & Access Control\n\n--- SLIDE 16 ---\n\nLLM Security & Privacy\u000b\nLLM inference runs entirely within Microsoft’s Azure boundary, with no data used for model training or shared with third parties and can be fully isolated from the public internet.\n\n--- SLIDE 17 ---\n\n04 \u000bCost Overview\n\n--- SLIDE 18 ---\n\nCosts are calculated for the West Europe region, are per month, assuming one daily run per site\nEstimated for Sites per month\n\n--- SLIDE 19 ---\n\n05 \u000bDesign Dependencies \n\n--- SLIDE 20 ---\n\nDependencies\nMitigation\nTopic\nThe following items highlight known design dependencies and operational considerations that have been accounted for in the proposed solution, along with corresponding mitigations.\nDesign Dependencies & Mitigations\n\n--- SLIDE 21 ---\n\n06 \u000bUpcoming Milestones\n\n--- SLIDE 22 ---\n\nUpcoming Milestones\n\n--- SLIDE 23 ---\n\n\n--- SLIDE 24 ---\n\nTemplate Message\n\n--- SLIDE 25 ---\n\nExample message\nRecommendation\nTheme + Prioritisation\nLink to Lumina\nSummary\nFocus",

Most styles should have an elasticity in range, and more than 80% of total units sold should come from styles within that range.\nChallenges: 262,730 styles. Current methodology have only 16% of styles with elasticities in range, and major styles are associated with poor model performance.\nBlend developed a solution based on demand forecasting models in three steps:\nStep 1: Model at the style level: one model per style.\nStep 2: Styles that don’t have enough data or model performance is low are grouped into broader categories based on common attributes, and then are modeled at the group level.\nStep 3: Styles that still don’t have an elasticity in range go to an imputation step: regression model.\nImproved model performance by an average of 32% based on SMAPE metrics\nImproved style coverage up to:\n18% with style level model: 83% of units sold covered\n38% adding group level model: 93% of units sold coverage\n100% adding imputation: 100% of units sold covered\n\n--- SLIDE 21 ---\n\nSeasonal\u000bMarkdown with Price Optimization\nThe business faced significant challenges in forecasting and\u000ballocating seasonal products, such as beach chairs, Halloween costumes, and Christmas gifts, due to lengthy supply chain lead times. These one-time orders necessitated cautious ordering to prevent customer dissatisfaction, often resulting in excess inventory. This surplus typically underwent a prolonged markdown process, impacting profitability and \u000binventory management strategies, highlighting the need for improved forecasting and pricing strategy to minimize waste and maximize profitability.\nGiven the seasonal products in inventory without replenishment, we aimed to determine the best pricing strategy for the four-week season to maximize customer satisfaction and profitability.\n\nWe developed a two-phase solution using both Linear Regression analysis and Linear Programming to find a solution for the markdown price problem that maximizes profits and minimizes write-offs during the 4-week markdown period:\nThe initial step involved training a regression model to determine Price Elasticity, gauging how demand reacts to changes in price.\nThe second step aimed to identify the weekly optimal markdown price combination for the 4-week markdown period, maximizing profits and minimizing write-offs using an optimization model​.\n\nTesting 3,400 stores with 650 items saved approximately \u000b$450,000 compared to the control group, which was attributed to improved margins and reduced write-offs. \nThis translated to ~$5MM network-wide net profit across five major seasons. \nA top retail pharmacy and healthcare company\n\n--- SLIDE 22 ---\n\nWrite Off Mitigation\nSome amount of write offs is expected, but recent years write off has significantly Sales Material\n\n--- SLIDE 86 ---\n\nPredictive maintenance relies on data from assets collected during normal operation periods and aims to predict when maintenance will be required, maximising the lifespan of different assets, mitigating against unplanned downtime and reducing operational costs. \nPredictive maintenance is a proactive maintenance strategy that tries to predict when a piece of equipment might fail so that maintenance work can be performed just before that happens.\nPredictive maintenance programs have been shown to lead to a tenfold increase in ROI, a 25%-30% reduction in maintenance costs, a 70%-75% decrease of breakdowns and a 35%-45% reduction in downtime.\nWHAT IS PREDICTIVE ASSET MAINTENANCE?\nbenefits\nMaintenance strategies\n\n--- SLIDE 87 ---\n\nHOW WE DELIVER other relevant stakeholders to ensure goals are met at every step of the way.\nData is collected from all sensors available\nModel is evaluated in a live operational environment \nMulti-asset optimisation brings together the outputs of multiple PAM models to inform Next Best Action\n\n--- SLIDE 89 ---\n\nThe Right data, at the right time, in the right hands\n\n--- SLIDE 90 ---\n\nThe Right The client also required the ability to simulate various future scenarios by adjusting external factors, to understand potential financial impacts. The company struggles with working capital and direct labor requirements due to the challenges in accurately predicting demand, which can lead to operational difficulties.\nBlend developed a solution that integrates historical financial data and dozens of external market factors (e.g., interest rates, CPI) to forecast demand and financial outcomes using plant level what-if scenario planning.\nTo ensure the models remain relevant, a dynamic training mechanism was implemented, keeping them consistently updated with the latest changes. All functionalities are seamlessly integrated into an intuitive user interface powered by  Streamlit. \nIncreased forecast time horizon from 3 months to 18 months\nReduced forecast error by 50% by meticulously selecting the optimal model for superior predictive accuracy. \nForecast EBITDA level results at ~70 individual plants\nA customised solution that enables easy expansion for other use cases (e.g. P&L and manpower calculations)\nBlend Created a Forecasting System Enabling More Accurate and Long-Term Forecasts for Demand To Better Budget and Resource Plan\nCONFIDENTIAL\n\n--- SLIDE 96 ---\n\nModels trained to predict future business demand at the most granular level possible. The levels can be thought of as a tree-like structure, where each level represents a different aggregation of the data:\nForecasts will need to be coherent across the aggregation structure. That is, we require forecasts to add up in a manner that is consistent with the aggregation structure of the collection of time series:\n\nBottom-up:  This approach involves first generating forecasts for each series at the bottom-level, and then summing these to produce forecasts for all the series in the structure\n\nTop-down first generating forecasts for the Total series and then disaggregating these down the hierarchy\n\nOptimal reconciliation will occur if we can find the  ‘sweet spot’ that minimises the forecast error of the set of coherent forecasts\n\n\n--- SLIDE 164 ---\n\nTime Series: Decomposition\u000bSupercharge your Supply Chain to deliver end-to-end care for every individual\u000b\nStandard trend\nSeasonality and Cyclical component\nRandom Noise\nThe decomposition of time series is a statistical task that deconstructs a time series into several components, each representing one of the underlying categories of pattern; It seeks to construct, from an observed time series, a number of component series\n\nTime series will be decomposed into different components; this will allow the appropriate methodology to be applied. Traditionally, there are 3 components, basic trend, a seasonal component and random noise. In reality, there are additional factors that can influence future demand:\nHistorical Sales Data\nPrescription Trends\nSeasonality\nDrug Lifecycles\nNatural and unexplained variance\nIntervention effects\nRegulatory changes\nInsurance coverage\n\n--- SLIDE 165 ---\n\nReplenishment and Redistribution\u000bDemand Driven inventory planning\nGranular forecasts will be used to determine and plan for the estimated demand; this will allow robust decisions, taking into account the current stock situation:\n\n--- SLIDE 166 ---\n\nReplenishment & Redistribution\u000bData driven Inventory Monitoring and Replenishment models\u000b\nManage the movement of stock from one location to another, to ensure that stock continues to flow efficiently along your Supply Chain. Inventory replenishment aims to use the most efficient methods to move inventory fast and efficiently.\nSelecting the right inventory policy depends on various factors, including the type of products, demand patterns, supply chain structure, and business objectives.  It requires\nOften, a combination of these policies is needed to meet the specific needs and challenges. The effectiveness of these policies is enhanced when they are supported by accurate data, technology, and well-defined processes.\nMulti-Echelon Inventory Optimization: This strategy considers inventory management across multiple locations or levels in the supply chain to optimize inventory distribution.\nCritical Inventory Policy: Critical drugs, that require special attention ensuring their continuous availability to avoid disruptions\n\nMin-Max Policy:  Maintained within a range (minimum and maximum levels). When inventory reaches the minimum level, a replenishment order is placed to bring it up to the maximum level.\nABC Analysis: Inventory is categorized into three (or more) groups based on their importance, enabling effective management\n\nSafety Stock Policy: Safety stock is additional inventory kept as a buffer against variations in demand and lead time. The safety stock level is based on the desired service level.\n\n--- SLIDE 167 ---\n\nPredictive Asset Maintenance for a Global Production and Exploration Company \nUsing data to predict what is We propose a two-stage model structure to capture this dynamic:\nTransit stage: Estimated the effect of impressions on transits by variable channel by aggregating customer panel data across regions and time. We regress transits of variable channels on TV and Digital impressions controlling for seasonality, regional fixed effects and other factors.\nConversion stage: To derive the lower funnel impact of TV and Digital POLV, we used a Machine Learning Attribution model applied to customer individual data. We proposed a two-stage structure to capture this dynamic:\nFIRST STAGE\nAdvertising impressions from offline or online (variable or fixed) lead to transits through online channels. \nSECOND (TRANSIT) STAGE\nAny impact of mass advertising is necessarily mediated through one or multiple online channels. Customers who are influenced by mass advertising must transit in order to engage.\n*Variable marketing channels include Amazon Keywords, Amazon Associates, Browser Extension, Display Advertising, Dynamic Advertising, Free search, Mobile Preloads, Paid Social, and Social Media. Fixed (or mass) marketing channels include TV, Print, OOH, Radio, Online Video/Display\nEstimates from the transit and conversion stages together permit simulation of the conversions that would have occurred if a given channel had not been in operation. Comparing the outcomes between such a simulation and the actual conversions provides an estimate of the incremental lift for the channel.\n\nRESULT: ESTIMATE CAUSAL EFFECT\nDEVELOPED CROSS-CHANNEL MEASUREMENT CAPABILITIES FOR A LARGE E-COMMERCE RETAILER Retail: Cross-Channel Measurement\n1",
